title: Absorbance Formula Calculator + Beer-Lambert Test
description: Solve the absorbance formula A = ebc for any variable and convert absorbance to transmittance, then test yourself on six questions built from this page.
intro: Six questions on the formula above: which variable you are solving for, where path length goes, and why transmittance does not fall in a straight line.

questions.q: The tool's defaults are A = 0.6, ε = 6000 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ and b = 1 cm. Solve for the concentration c.
options: 3600 M, from ε × b × A instead
0.600 M, taking c as A when b = 1
questions.why: Concentration is the one variable you divide for, c = A / (εb), so multiplying the three defaults together answers a different question entirely.
questions.source: Worked example 1 on the page: c = A / (ε × b) = 0.6 / (6000 × 1) = 0.0001 M = 1.00 × 10⁻⁴ M = 100 µM. Distractor 0 is 6000 × 1 × 0.6 = 3600.

questions.q: What does this page give as the units of molar absorptivity ε?
options: M cm, molar times path length
None, ε is unitless like A
cm⁻¹ only, A has no units
questions.why: ε is per molar per centimetre, which is exactly what cancels the M of concentration and the cm of path length and leaves absorbance with no units.
questions.source: Page FAQ: 'What are the units of molar absorptivity (ε)? M⁻¹cm⁻¹, per molar, per centimeter.' The formula block lists ε = molar absorptivity (M-1 cm-1) and A = absorbance (no units).

questions.q: You read a sample in a 0.5 cm microcuvette but leave b = 1 cm in the calculation. What happens to the concentration you report?
options: Twice too high, b divides out
Four times too low, b squares
Twice too low, A was halved
questions.why: Path length multiplies absorbance exactly as concentration does, so halving the cuvette halves the reading and a calculation still assuming 1 cm hands back half the real concentration.
questions.source: Page formula block: b = path length (cm, usually 1 cm for a standard cuvette), and c = A / (εb). Using the page's NADH figures, A at 0.5 cm is 6220 × 0.5 × 50e-6 = 0.1555, and 0.1555 / (6220 × 1) = 2.5e-5 M, half of the true 5e-5 M.

questions.q: A reading of A = 0.6 works out to what percent transmittance?
questions.why: Transmittance falls logarithmically with absorbance, so A = 0.6 still lets about a quarter of the light through rather than the 40% you get by treating A as a straight fraction absorbed.
questions.source: Page converter, worked: %T = 100 × 10⁻⁰·⁶ = 25.12%, and the converter ships with A = 0.6 against %T = 25.1. Recomputed: 100 × 10^(−0.6) = 25.119.

questions.q: A 0.0002 M solution reads A = 0.85 in a 1 cm cuvette. What is its molar absorptivity?
options: 4250 M cm, since ε is M times cm
questions.why: Molar absorptivity is measured by dividing a known reading by path length and concentration, and its units have to come out reciprocal, so an answer in M cm is wrong before the arithmetic is checked.
questions.source: Practice problem 1 on the page: ε = A / (b × c) = 0.85 / (1 × 0.0002) = 4250 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. Distractor 1 is 0.85 × 1 × 0.0002 = 0.00017; distractor 3 is 0.85 / (1 × 0.002) = 425.

questions.q: A spectrophotometer reads 10% transmittance. What absorbance is that, and why does this page single the value out?
options: 0.100, since 10% is one tenth of it
2.303, using ln rather than log base 10
questions.why: Every unit of absorbance is a tenfold cut in transmitted light, so 10% through is exactly A = 1, which is the point the page says readings start pulling away from linearity.
questions.source: Practice problem 2 on the page: A = −log₁₀(T) = −log₁₀(10/100) = −log₁₀(0.10) = 1.000, plus the FAQ line that above roughly A = 1 the reading deviates from strict linearity. Recomputed: −log10(0.1) = 1.0.
